newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Sing Tao silent on sale reports.
newsitem.headline: HK's Sing Tao silent on sale reports.

text.p: Executives of newspaper publisher and printer Sing Tao Holdings Ltd remained silent on Wednesday on reports the company would be sold and declined to say why trading in its shares had been suspended.

"No comment," said Lawrence Wong, group general manager, when asked about unconfirmed reports that chairman Sally Aw was in talks with Malaysia's Hong Leong group to sell all or part of her 68 percent holding in Sing Tao.
Trading in Sing Tao shares was suspended on Wednesday morning at the company's request pending an announcement, the Hong Kong stock exchange said.
On Tuesday, the shares rose HK$0.40 to HK$3.80.
Company secretary Seaman Kwok said Sing Tao's three executive directors were out of town and unavailable for comment.
Hong Leong group executives were not immediately available for comment.
At the pre-suspension share price of HK$3.80, Sing Tao has a total market capitalisation of HK$1.6163 billion. The Aw family's 68 percent stake is worth HK$1.1 billion.
Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee Hwa is a director of the Sing Tao Holdings company and his family is beneficially interested in 68,280 shares worth HK$259,464.
The company publishes the Chinese-language Sing Tao Daily and the English-language Hongkong Standard. Until December last year, the company also published an evening paper.
The Chinese-language Sing Tao Evening Post was closed on December 17, 1996 after incurring losses in the year ended March 1996 and the six months ended September 1996.
Along with other newspaper publishers, the company has suffered from the downturn and contraction of the industry in Hong Kong, as well as a period of intense price competiton in the past two years.
Although the cycle looked like it had bottomed out, it might still be early days for the owners to hope to get a fair price for the company, analysts said.
"The business cycle is moving in Sing Tao's favour but its franchise appears to be under structural pressure at every level," said Asia Equity analyst James Miles in a March report on the company.
"Sing Tao Daily's traditional niche in property (advertising) is being eroded by other more progressive publishers," said Miles.
"The environment for Sing Tao's newspapers overseas -- which account for 30 percent of publishing revenues -- has also become considerably more competitive in the last few years."
The company reported profit attributable to shareholders of HK$4.92 million for the six months ended September 1996.
And while this was a 76.2 percent decline over the year-earlier period, it looked to be a turnaround from the HK$146.4 million loss reported for the year ended March 1996.
The savings derived from the closure of the Sing Tao Evening Post, which was losing HK$3 million a month, should be fully realised in the 1998 financial year, the company said.
Analysts have revised upwards their forecasts for the company for 1997 and 1998.
Asia Equity's Miles is forecasting earnings of HK$4.5 million, up from a previously forecast loss of HK$35.1 million.
The consensus forecast is for attributable profit of HK$59.5 million in 1997 and HK$148.9 million in 1998.
Wong said Sing Tao's accounts for the year ended March 31 were now being audited but would not say when the results would be released.
The company reported its final results on August 9 last year.
